title: Feedback and margins
summary: Why close the loop, what the sensitivity 1/(1 + T_L) says and what the phase and gain margins measure.
text: On its own, the buck regulates poorly: a step in the duty makes the output overshoot by 80 % of the jump and ring for 1.7 ms ( Second-order pair and quality factor Q ), and the gain changes with the input and the load. Feedback measures the output, compares it with the reference and corrects the duty. One trip around the loop goes through the controller, the plant and the sensor: \[T_L(s) = G_c(s)\,G_{vd}(s)\,H\tag{1}\] ≡ In this course's converters, the ADC reads the output voltage itself, and \(H = 1\) . What the loop buys: the sensitivity \[S(s) = \frac{1}{1 + T_L(s)}, \qquad \frac{T_L(s)}{1 + T_L(s)} = 1 - S(s)\tag{2}\] ≡ Where \(|T_L|\) is large, a disturbance at the output comes out divided by \(|1 + T_L|\) , and the output follows the reference. Where \(|T_L|\) is small, \(S \approx 1\) : the loop does not act. Near the crossover, \(|1 + T_L|\) can be less than 1, and the loop amplifies the disturbance. That is the price of bandwidth. Crossover and margins Crossover frequency \(f_c\) : where \(|T_L| = 1\) , or 0 dB, with the magnitude falling. In order of magnitude, it is the loop's bandwidth. Phase margin (PM): \(180^\circ + \angle T_L\) at \(f_c\) . Gain margin (GM): how far, in dB, \(|T_L|\) is from 1 where the phase passes −180°. Both measure the distance from \(T_L\) to the point \(-1\) , where the loop oscillates by itself, and both read in a concrete way: the PM is the extra delay the loop tolerates, \(\Delta t = \mathrm{PM}/(360^\circ f_c)\) , and the GM is the extra gain it tolerates. A delay is not a pole \[\varphi_d(f) = -360^\circ\, f\, t_d, \qquad t_d = (1 + D)\,T_s\tag{3}\] ≡ A pure delay, \(e^{-s t_d}\) , has a magnitude of 1 and a phase that falls in a straight line with \(f\) , without limit. A pole changes the magnitude, and its phase stops at −90°. The delay is not a × in the s-plane, but it eats more margin the higher the crossover. loading the figure… The buck's loop gain with the 2p2z: read the crossover, the phase margin and the gain margin, and move the crossover to watch the margins fall. In the converters In the buck, with the 2p2z, the loop crosses at 8 kHz with a PM of 41° and a GM of 13.9 dB ( Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins ). From the model, \(|T_L| = 7.7\) at 100 Hz: a disturbance at that frequency reaches the output divided by 7.9 ( \(|S|\) = −17.9 dB). At 8 kHz, \(|S| = 1.42\) (+3 dB): there the loop amplifies. The worst point is 9.8 kHz, where \(T_L\) comes within 0.62 of the point \(-1\) . Extra delay tolerated: \(41^\circ/(360^\circ \cdot 8\,\text{kHz}) = 14.2\) µs, about 2.8 periods at 200 kHz. The delay the loop already has, \((1 + D)T_s = 6.875\) µs, takes 19.8° at 8 kHz ( Computation and PWM delay ). Extra gain tolerated: 13.9 dB, or 4.95 times. What the 41° margin means for the load step, and why the rule of thumb for damping misses here, is in From margin to damping: the ζ ≈ PM/100 rule and where it fails . title: First-order pole and zero
summary: A real pole brings the magnitude down at −20 dB per decade and lags the phase to −90°; a zero does the opposite. In time, the pole is an exponential with time constant 1/ωₚ.
text: Almost every useful system is a product of first- and second-order blocks. This note covers the first-order ones: a real pole and a real zero, in standard form . The pole \[G(s) = \frac{1}{1 + s/\omega_p}, \qquad |G(j\omega)| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + (\omega/\omega_p)^2}}, \qquad \angle G(j\omega) = -\arctan\frac{\omega}{\omega_p}\tag{1}\] ≡ In the Bode plot, the pole reads as three straight lines, the asymptotes : well below \(\omega_p\) , the magnitude stays at 0 dB and the phase at 0°; well above, the magnitude falls 20 dB per decade (ten times smaller each decade) and the phase tends to −90° ; at \(\omega_p\) itself, the real curve passes 3 dB below the asymptotes' corner, and the phase is exactly −45° . The phase changes almost entirely within one decade each side: −5.7° at \(\omega_p/10\) and −84.3° at \(10\,\omega_p\) . −3 dB is not half At \(\omega_p\) , the magnitude is \(1/\sqrt 2 = 0.707\) . Half, 0.5, is −6 dB, and happens at \(\sqrt 3\,\omega_p\) . In time, the unit step response is an exponential: \[y(t) = 1 - e^{-t/\tau}, \qquad \tau = \frac{1}{\omega_p}\] It reaches 63 % of the final value at \(\tau\) , 95 % at \(3\tau\) and 98 % at \(4\tau\) . The 2 % settling time is therefore \(4\tau\) . The further the pole from the origin (the larger \(\omega_p\) ), the faster the response. loading the figure… A real pole: drag it along the real axis and watch the pole frequency in the Bode plot and the time constant in the step. The zero The zero, \(1 + s/\omega_z\) , mirrors the pole: the magnitude rises 20 dB per decade above \(\omega_z\) , and the phase leads up to +90°, passing +45° at \(\omega_z\) . Alone it is improper: the gain would grow without bound, and the response to a step would hold an impulse, because \(s\) is a derivative. In a circuit, every zero comes with poles that limit the gain at high frequency. Together with a pole, \((1 + s/\omega_z)/(1 + s/\omega_p)\) , it becomes a buildable block, and that is how zeros appear in compensators ( PI, phase lead and the type III ). loading the figure… A real zero alone: the figure adds a far pole, ten times further out, so that the step exists. The integrator With the pole at the origin, \(G(s) = \omega_p/s\) , there is no plateau: the magnitude falls 20 dB per decade at all frequencies, crosses 0 dB at \(\omega_p\) , and the phase stays at −90°. The step response is a ramp that never stops rising. It is a compensator's integral action, the one that brings the steady-state error to zero ( PI, phase lead and the type III ). In the converters The ESR zero is a real zero: \[f_{\mathrm{ESR}} = \frac{1}{2\pi\,R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\,C}\tag{2}\] ≡ In the buck, with 47 µF and 5 mΩ, it sits at 677 kHz. At 8 kHz, the 2p2z's crossover, it adds 0.7° of phase; at 100 kHz, half the sampling frequency, 8.4°. In the boost and the buck-boost, with 100 µF and 10 mΩ, it sits at 159 kHz. The buck's 2p2z has both kinds of block. The pole at 60 kHz takes only 0.08 dB and 7.6° at 8 kHz; its time constant is 2.65 µs

title: From margin to damping: the ζ ≈ PM/100 rule and where it fails
summary: How the phase margin turns into damping and overshoot, over what range the ζ ≈ PM/100 rule holds, and why it misses in the buck with the 2p2z.
text: The phase margin says how far the loop is from oscillating ( Feedback and margins ). What the oscilloscope shows, though, is the step: how far it overshoots the target and for how long it rings. This note bridges the two, and shows in the buck where the bridge gives way. From margin to step Near the crossover, many loops look like an integrator followed by a pole, \(T_L = \omega_n^2/[s\,(s + 2\zeta\omega_n)]\) . This course's buck is not one of them, as shown below. Closed, this loop is exactly a second-order pair , and the phase margin depends only on the damping: \(\mathrm{PM} = \arctan\big(2\zeta/\sqrt{\sqrt{1 + 4\zeta^4} - 2\zeta^2}\big)\) . \(\zeta\) \(Q\) PM PM/100 Overshoot 0.2 2.5 22.6° 0.23 53 % 0.4 1.25 43.1° 0.43 25 % 0.6 0.83 59.2° 0.59 9.5 % 0.7 0.71 65.2° 0.65 4.6 % 0.8 0.63 69.9° 0.70 1.5 % Hence the rule \(\zeta \approx \mathrm{PM}/100\) , with PM in degrees. In the integrator-plus-pole loop, it is off by less than 10 % between 37° and 67.5° of margin and by less than 15 % at any margin up to 71°; the error vanishes at 57.4°. Below that, the rule promises a little more damping than there is; above, a little less. That range belongs to the model loop, not to any loop. With \(\zeta\) , the \(Q = 1/(2\zeta)\) and the overshoot follow from the pair's standard form: \[G(s) = \frac{1}{1 + \dfrac{s}{Q\,\omega_0} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_0^2}}, \qquad s_{1,2} = -\frac{\omega_0}{2Q} \pm j\,\omega_0\sqrt{1 - \frac{1}{4Q^2}}, \qquad Q = \frac{1}{2\zeta}\tag{1}\] ≡ A real loop has more poles. The pair near the crossover is dominant when the others are at least five times further from the \(j\omega\) axis (ten, to trust the numbers) and no zero sits near it: then the step rings near \(f_c\) with the table's overshoot. When a pole sits closer to the axis than the pair, it rules the slow response. In the converters In the buck, with the 2p2z, the loop crosses at 8 kHz with a PM of 41° ( Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins ). Damping. Predict: with a PM of 41°, the rule gives \(\zeta \approx 0.41\) , \(Q \approx 1.2\) and about 25 % overshoot. Check: the closed-loop model gives a pair at 7.2 kHz with \(\zeta = 0.31\) ( \(Q \approx 1.6\) , 35 % overshoot): the rule promises a third more damping than there is. In QSPICE, the 1 to 2 A load step drops the output to 8.59 V, and it swings back to 9.14 V ( The 2p2z compensator ): the swing back is 35 % of the dip, what \(\zeta \approx 0.31\) predicts. Why the rule misses here. It assumes two things, and the buck meets neither. First, that the loop near the crossover is an integrator followed by a pole; the buck's is the plant near −180°, plus the compensator's lead and the firmware's delay. Not even the table's exact formula gets it right: with 41.3°, it gives \(\zeta = 0.38\) . Second, that the pair is dominant. title: PI, phase lead and the type III
summary: The integrator brings the steady-state error to zero and costs 90° of phase; phase lead gives phase back at the crossover; the type III is an integrator with two leads, and the 2p2z is its digital relative.
text: A compensator is made of the same first-order blocks as the plant, chosen to give the loop gain two things: high gain at low frequency and enough phase at the crossover. The integrator: zero steady-state error With the loop closed, the steady-state error to a reference step is \(1/(1 + T_L(0))\) . If the compensator is just a gain \(K\) , \(T_L(0) = K\,G_{vd}(0)\) is finite, and some error always remains. In the buck, \(G_{vd}(0) = 23.9\) : for less than 1 % error, \(K\) would have to exceed 4, and the crossover would go where the phase leaves no margin. A pole at the origin, \(K_I/s\) , makes \(T_L(0)\) infinite, and the error to a step goes to zero . The price is the integrator's phase, −90° at every frequency, which adds to the plant's. The PI: integrator plus a zero \[G_c(s) = K_I\,\frac{1 + s/\omega_z}{s}\] The zero gives phase back above \(\omega_z\) : well above it, the PI behaves like a gain, with phase near 0°. With the zero a decade below the crossover, the integrator barely weighs on the margin. But the PI never gives positive phase, and the buck, above resonance, is already near −180°. Phase lead \[G_c(s) = \frac{1 + s/\omega_z}{1 + s/\omega_p}, \qquad \alpha = \frac{\omega_p}{\omega_z} > 1, \qquad \sin\varphi_{\max} = \frac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha + 1}\] It is a zero followed by a higher pole. Between the two, the magnitude rises 20 dB per decade and the phase forms a hill, with the peak \(\varphi_{\max}\) at the geometric mean, \(\sqrt{\omega_z\,\omega_p}\) . The peak is placed on the crossover. Lead has diminishing returns: \(\alpha\) 2 4 9 16 100 \(\varphi_{\max}\) 19.5° 36.9° 53.1° 61.9° 78.6° Each lead costs gain at high frequency, \(20\log_{10}\alpha\) , which amplifies noise and ripple. For the same phase, two smaller leads always cost less gain than a single one, and the difference grows with the phase: 9.2 against 9.5 dB for 30°, 19.1 against 22.9 dB for 60°, 26.5 against 42.3 dB for 80°. The type III: integrator plus two leads The analog type III compensator of a voltage-mode buck is an integrator with two leads, usually equal: \[G_c(s) = \frac{K\,\omega_0}{s}\left(\frac{1 + s/\omega_0}{1 + s/\omega_p}\right)^2\] The two zeros sit near the LC resonance, where the plant takes up to 180°, and give up to 180° of phase, minus what the poles take; the two poles limit the gain above the crossover. loading the figure… The buck's loop gain with the 2p2z: move the zeros and the pole and watch the phase margin; the gain is recomputed to keep the crossover. In the converters The buck's 2p2z has an integrator, two zeros at 2 kHz and one pole at 60 kHz: one high-frequency pole fewer than the type III. title: Right-half-plane zero
summary: A zero right of the jω axis has an ordinary zero's magnitude and a pole's phase; it destabilises nothing, but makes the step start the wrong way and limits the crossover.
text: So far the zeros sat left of the \(j\omega\) axis, at \(s = -\omega_z\) . Flipping the sign, the zero moves to \(s = +\omega_z\) , the right half-plane : \[G(s) = 1 - \frac{s}{\omega_z}\] The magnitude does not see the side; the phase does At \(s = j\omega\) , the magnitude is \(\sqrt{1 + (\omega/\omega_z)^2}\) , the same as an ordinary zero 's: it rises 20 dB per decade above \(\omega_z\) . The phase is \(-\arctan(\omega/\omega_z)\) : instead of leading up to +90°, it falls to −90°, like a pole's. A pole's phase, a zero's magnitude An ordinary pole and a right-half-plane zero both take 90° of phase. The difference is in the magnitude: the pole brings the gain down, the right-half-plane zero raises it. For the loop it is the worst combination: more gain and less phase at the same time. It is not an unstable pole Stability depends only on the poles. A system with all its poles on the left and a zero on the right is stable: its step response settles. It is non-minimum phase : it has more phase lag than the function with the same magnitude and the zero mirrored to the left, the minimum-phase one. What the zero changes in time is the start. Right after the step, the output moves the opposite way to its final value, and only then turns around: this is the inverse initial response . loading the figure… Two poles and a zero at 2 kHz: the button mirrors the zero between the half-planes. The magnitude does not change; the phase and the step's start do. Why it limits the crossover A compensator cancels an ordinary zero by putting a pole on top of it. To cancel a right-half-plane zero it would need a right-half-plane pole: an unstable controller. That is not done. What is left is to cross well below the zero, where its lag \(\arctan(f_c/f_z)\) is still small and phase margin is left. The rules of thumb range from \(f_c < f_z/3\) , which costs 18.4°, to \(f_c < f_z/5\) , which costs 11.3°, depending on the source and on whether the nominal zero or the worst-case one is used. When the compensator puts its zeros at \(f_0\) , the resonance, and crosses above \(3f_0\) , the window \(3f_0 < f_c < f_z/3\) exists only if \(f_z/f_0 > 9\) ; in the lossless boost, \(f_z/f_0\) is the pole pair's own \(Q\) , and in the lab, at 10 V and 2 A, the window is empty. In the converters In the boost, raising the duty keeps the inductor disconnected from the output for longer; at the first instant the output receives less current and falls. title: Second-order pair and quality factor Q
summary: A pole pair is described by f₀ and Q; in the Bode plot, Q is the height of the resonant peak, and in the s-plane and the step it is the balance between oscillation and decay.
text: The buck's LC filter stores energy in two elements, and the energy flows from one to the other: the response oscillates. A first-order pole never oscillates; that takes a pair. The standard form \[G(s) = \frac{1}{1 + \dfrac{s}{Q\,\omega_0} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_0^2}}, \qquad s_{1,2} = -\frac{\omega_0}{2Q} \pm j\,\omega_0\sqrt{1 - \frac{1}{4Q^2}}, \qquad Q = \frac{1}{2\zeta}\tag{1}\] ≡ Two numbers describe the pair: \(f_0\) , the pair's frequency: the poles' distance from the origin, in hertz in the \(s/2\pi\) plane; \(Q\) , the quality factor: how lightly damped the pair is. The textbooks' classical form uses the damping ratio \(\zeta\) ; the bridge is \(Q = 1/(2\zeta)\) . This course uses \(Q\) , because it reads straight off the Bode plot. Where the poles sit The value of \(Q\) decides the roots' shape: \(Q < 0.5\) : two distinct real poles, no oscillation; \(Q = 0.5\) : a double real pole at \(-\omega_0\) ; \(Q > 0.5\) : a complex conjugate pair. The larger \(Q\) , the closer to the \(j\omega\) axis; \(Q \to \infty\) : the poles sit on the axis, at \(\pm j\omega_0\) , and the response oscillates forever. For a complex pair, the imaginary part, \(\approx f_0\) when \(Q\) is large, is the oscillation's frequency, and the real part, \(f_0/(2Q)\) , is the decay: the envelope falls with time constant \(2Q/\omega_0\) . In the Bode plot below \(f_0\) , the magnitude stays at the DC gain, and the phase near 0°; at \(f_0\) , the phase passes −90°, and the magnitude is about \(Q\) times the DC gain, or \(20\log_{10}Q\) dB above it. This resonant peak only shows with \(Q > 0.707\) ; above \(f_0\) , the magnitude falls 40 dB per decade , and the phase tends to −180° , in a transition about \(f_0/Q\) wide. In the step With a high \(Q\) , the response goes past the final value, comes back and rings around it. The overshoot is \[M_p = e^{-\pi/\sqrt{4Q^2 - 1}},\] 44 % with \(Q = 2\) , 16 % with \(Q = 1\) , 4.3 % with \(Q = 0.707\) and zero with \(Q \le 0.5\) . loading the figure… A pole pair with f₀ of 1 kHz: change Q with the control, or drag the pair, and watch the peak, the phase and the overshoot. In the converters The buck's LC, 22 µH and 47 µF, has \(f_0 = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC}) = 4.95\) kHz. The \(Q\) depends on the load, because the load across the capacitor damps the pair: \[f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}, \qquad Q \approx \frac{1}{\dfrac{Z_0}{R} + \dfrac{R_s + R_{\mathrm{ESR}}}{Z_0}}, \qquad Z_0 = \sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}\tag{2}\] ≡ Load Poles ( \(s/2\pi\) ) \(Q\) Peak Overshoot to a step in \(d\) \(2Q/\omega_0\) 4.5 Ω (2 A) \(-539 \pm j\,4939\) Hz 4.6 13.3 dB 71 % 0.30 ms 9 Ω (1 A) \(-351 \pm j\,4947\) Hz 7.1 17.0 dB 80 % 0.45 ms 90 Ω (0.1 A) \(-182 \pm j\,4947\) Hz 13.6 22.7 dB 89 % 0.88 ms The numbers come from the averaged model, without the loop: a step in the duty would make the buck's output overshoot by 80 % of the jump, ringing with a 202 µs period, and take 1.7 ms to settle within 2 %. title: Control basics
summary: Seven notes, in order, from what a transfer function is to the buck's compensator: poles, zeros, Q, margins, the right-half-plane zero and compensators.
text: This trail is the course's control refresher, to take in one go instead of note by note. Each step uses the numbers of the lab's converters. If you do not know where to begin, first answer the questions in Start here . Transfer function, poles and zeros : the buck's plant as a ratio of polynomials, with the DC gain, the poles and the zeros in standard form. First-order pole and zero : the simplest block, a real pole or zero, in the Bode plot and in the step. Second-order pair and quality factor Q : two poles together can oscillate, and the factor \(Q\) says how much; this is the buck's LC. Feedback and margins : with the plant understood, we close the loop and measure the distance to oscillation. From margin to damping: the ζ ≈ PM/100 rule and where it fails : the margin turns into damping and overshoot, and the buck shows where the rule of thumb fails. Right-half-plane zero : the zero on the wrong side of the plane, which the boost has and the buck does not, and why it limits the crossover. PI, phase lead and the type III : the blocks the compensator puts together for zero error and phase margin. End of the trail From here, go back to the converters: the From the analog buck to the digital loop trail takes the buck from the power stage to the firmware, and the From the boost to the digital loop shows what changes when the plant has the right-half-plane zero.

title: Transfer function, poles and zeros
summary: A transfer function is a ratio of two polynomials in s; the DC gain, the poles and the zeros, written in standard form, tell almost everything about the Bode plot and the step.
text: The note on the buck's plant arrives at this expression: \[G_{vd}(s) = \frac{\hat v_o(s)}{\hat d(s)} = V_{in}\,\frac{R}{R + R_s}\;\frac{1 + s/\omega_{\mathrm{ESR}}}{1 + \dfrac{s}{Q\,\omega_0} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_0^2}}\tag{1}\] ≡ If it looks like a closed box, start here. It has three pieces, and each has a name: a gain, a zero and a pair of poles. This note teaches you to recognise them. A ratio of polynomials In a linear time-invariant system, at rest at time zero, the Laplace transforms of the output and of the input keep a fixed ratio that depends only on the system: \[G(s) = \frac{Y(s)}{U(s)} = \frac{N(s)}{D(s)}\] In the buck, the input is the small change of the duty, \(\hat d\) , and the output is the small change of the output voltage, \(\hat v_o\) , around the operating point ( The averaged switch model ). Both polynomials have real coefficients, and their roots have names: zeros are the roots of the numerator \(N(s)\) : there, \(G(s) = 0\) ; poles are the roots of the denominator \(D(s)\) : there, \(G(s)\) goes to infinity; the order is the degree of \(D(s)\) . The buck is second order: it stores energy in two places, the inductor and the capacitor. In a passive circuit like this one, each pole points to an element that stores energy; the compensator and the firmware's delay do not follow that rule. A function whose numerator degree is less than or equal to the denominator's is proper , and only those exist in a circuit: the gain does not grow without bound at high frequency. DC gain At \(s = 0\) the function takes its DC gain (or static gain), the response to a constant input. In the buck, \(G_{vd}(0) = V_{in}\,R/(R + R_s) \approx V_{in}\) : each 1 % more duty raises the output by about 0.24 V. The standard form Each real root can be written as a factor \(1 + s/\omega\) , which is 1 at \(s = 0\) . A pole at \(s = -\omega_p\) becomes \(1/(1 + s/\omega_p)\) ; a zero at \(s = -\omega_z\) becomes \(1 + s/\omega_z\) . A pair of complex roots becomes \(1 + s/(Q\omega_0) + s^2/\omega_0^2\) ( Second-order pair and quality factor Q ). This is the standard form , and it has two advantages: the DC gain stands alone in front, because every factor is 1 at \(s = 0\) ; each \(\omega\) is the frequency where that factor starts to act: that is where it shows up in the Bode plot. In the form with \(s + a\) , such as \(K/(s + a)\) , the DC gain is \(K/a\) and stays hidden. That is why this course writes everything in standard form, like \(G_{vd}\) in (1) and the compensator \(C(s) = K_I(1 + s/\omega_{z1})(1 + s/\omega_{z2})/[s\,(1 + s/\omega_p)]\) of the 2p2z . Pole and zero frequency The root at \(s = -\omega\) corresponds to the frequency \(\omega\) , in rad/s, or \(f = \omega/2\pi\) , in Hz: the pole frequency or zero frequency. This course's figures mark the s-plane's axes in hertz, \(s/2\pi\) . The s-plane Each root is a point in the complex plane. title: The averaged switch model
summary: Replacing the switch pair by its average over one period turns the buck into a continuous circuit; perturbed and linearized, it gives the small-signal model.
text: To design the control we need a transfer function, but the switch turns on and off every \(T_s\) and has none. The way out is to look at the average of each quantity over one period, which varies slowly. This note does the derivation for the buck; the result is the plant of the next note . Step 1: the switched circuit Let \(q(t) \in \{0, 1\}\) be the state of the high-side switch. The switching-node voltage is \(v_{sw} = q\,v_{in}\) , and the current drawn from the input is \(i_{in} = q\,i_L\) . On the inductor, with \(R_s = R_L + R_{on}\) (in CCM there is always one switch in series with it): \[L\,\frac{di_L}{dt} = q\,v_{in} - v_o - R_s\,i_L\] Step 2: the average over one period Define the moving average \(\langle x \rangle_{T_s}(t) = \frac{1}{T_s}\int_{t - T_s}^{t} x(\tau)\,d\tau\) . The average of \(q\) is the duty ratio \(d\) . If \(v_{in}\) and \(i_L\) barely change within one period (small ripple), the average of the product is the product of the averages, and the switch pair becomes the averaged switching cell : \[\langle v_{sw} \rangle_{T_s} = d\,\langle v_{in} \rangle_{T_s}, \qquad \langle i_{in} \rangle_{T_s} = d\,\langle i_L \rangle_{T_s}\tag{1}\] ≡ Averaged switch model The averaged cell is an ideal transformer of ratio \(1 : d\) , with a variable \(d\) : the voltage comes out multiplied by \(d\) , and the input current is the inductor's multiplied by \(d\) . Power is conserved: \(\langle v_{in}\rangle\langle i_{in}\rangle = \langle v_{sw}\rangle\langle i_L\rangle\) . Replacing the cell in the circuit, the inductor equation becomes \[L\,\frac{d\langle i_L\rangle}{dt} = d\,\langle v_{in}\rangle - \langle v_o\rangle - R_s\,\langle i_L\rangle\] and the capacitor, the ESR and the load stay as before, with the averaged quantities. The ripple vanishes by construction. Step 3: the operating point In steady state, the derivatives vanish: \(\langle i_L\rangle = I_L = V_o/R\) and \(D\,V_{in} = V_o + R_s I_L\) , that is, \(D = \frac{V_o}{V_{in}}\cdot\frac{R + R_s}{R}\) , the duty ratio with losses. Step 4: perturbation Write each quantity as its operating point plus a small perturbation: \(d = D + \hat d\) , \(v_{in} = V_{in} + \hat v_{in}\) , \(i_L = I_L + \hat i_L\) , \(v_o = V_o + \hat v_o\) . The only nonlinear term is the product \(d\,v_{in}\) : \[d\,v_{in} = D V_{in} + V_{in}\,\hat d + D\,\hat v_{in} + \hat d\,\hat v_{in}\] Step 5: linearization The term \(\hat d\,\hat v_{in}\) is the product of two small perturbations and is neglected. Subtracting the operating point leaves a linear equation: \[L\,\frac{d\hat i_L}{dt} = V_{in}\,\hat d + D\,\hat v_{in} - \hat v_o - R_s\,\hat i_L\] The switching node becomes a source \(\hat v_{sw} = V_{in}\hat d + D\hat v_{in}\) that drives the LC filter. title: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
summary: In steady state, the volt-second balance on the inductor gives the buck's duty ratio, and the triangular current gives the current and voltage ripple.
text: The buck connects the switching node to the input, then to ground, and the LC filter delivers the average of that square wave to the load. This note computes the duty ratio and the ripple in steady state. It is the first step of the digital buck trail . V in Q1 Q2 L C R V out firmware HG LG PWM ADC Synchronous buck: the high-side switch conducts for D·Tₛ and the low-side switch for the rest of the period. Volt-second balance In steady state, the inductor current ends each period at the value it started with. Since \(v_L = L\,di_L/dt\) , the area of the inductor voltage over one period is zero: \[(V_{in} - V_o)\,D T_s + (-V_o)(1 - D)\,T_s = 0\] With the high-side switch closed, the inductor sees \(V_{in} - V_o\) ; with it open (and the low-side switch closed), it sees \(-V_o\) . Solving: \[D = \frac{V_o}{V_{in}}\tag{1}\] ≡ Duty ratio The duty ratio \(D\) is the fraction of the switching period \(T_s = 1/f_s\) during which the high-side switch conducts. We write \(D' = 1 - D\) for the rest of the period. The resistive losses ( \(R_s = R_L + R_{on}\) , in series with the inductor) call for slightly more \(D\) , because part of the voltage drops across them. In closed loop this does not matter: the controller finds the \(D\) that gives \(V_o\) on its own. Inductor current ripple During \(DT_s\) , the current rises with slope \((V_{in} - V_o)/L\) ; during \(D'T_s\) , it falls with slope \(V_o/L\) . The peak-to-peak ripple is \[\Delta i_L = \frac{(V_{in} - V_o)\,D}{L\,f_s} = \frac{V_o\,(1 - D)}{L\,f_s}\tag{2}\] ≡ The average of \(i_L\) is the load current \(I_o = V_o/R\) , because in steady state the capacitor accumulates no charge. The peak, \(I_o + \Delta i_L/2\) , is what saturates the core and what the switches must withstand. The boundary of continuous conduction Continuous conduction mode (CCM) In CCM, the inductor current never rests at zero during the period. The boundary is \(I_o = \Delta i_L/2\) : below it, the valley of the triangular wave would reach zero. In a buck with a diode, below the boundary the diode blocks and the converter enters discontinuous conduction (DCM), with another duty ratio and other dynamics. The synchronous buck is different: the low-side switch conducts in both directions, the current goes negative in the valley and the converter stays in CCM, called forced CCM. The equations of this note hold at any load. Negative current in the synchronous buck At light load, or in a downward reference step, the negative current returns energy to the input. A bench supply that cannot sink current may see its voltage rise. Controllers with "diode emulation" turn the low-side switch off when the current reaches zero, and the converter then enters DCM again. Output voltage ripple The capacitor absorbs the AC part of \(i_L\) , a triangle of \(\pm\Delta i_L/2\) . title: The ESR zero
summary: The output capacitor's series resistance adds a zero to the plant; with electrolytics it helps the loop, with ceramics it lies above the switching frequency and does not count.
text: A real capacitor has an equivalent series resistance (ESR). In the buck's plant , it appears as the factor \(1 + s/\omega_{\mathrm{ESR}}\) in the numerator of (1) : a real zero in the left half-plane. \[G_{vd}(s) = \frac{\hat v_o(s)}{\hat d(s)} = V_{in}\,\frac{R}{R + R_s}\;\frac{1 + s/\omega_{\mathrm{ESR}}}{1 + \dfrac{s}{Q\,\omega_0} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_0^2}}\tag{1}\] ≡ \[f_{\mathrm{ESR}} = \frac{1}{2\pi\,R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\,C}\tag{2}\] ≡ Where the zero comes from The impedance of the capacitor with its ESR is \[Z_C(s) = R_{\mathrm{ESR}} + \frac{1}{sC} = \frac{1 + s R_{\mathrm{ESR}} C}{sC}\] Below \(f_{\mathrm{ESR}}\) , \(1/sC\) dominates, and the capacitor filters. Above it, \(R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\) dominates, and the capacitor becomes a resistor: the current ripple now produces a proportional voltage ripple, the \(R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\Delta i_L\) part of equation Output voltage ripple of the buck . ESR zero The ESR zero is the frequency at which the two parts of the capacitor's impedance have equal magnitude. Above it, the buck's plant falls 20 dB per decade instead of 40, and the phase rises by up to 90° relative to the pole pair alone. What the zero does on the Bode plot A left-half-plane zero lifts the phase: \(\arctan(f/f_{\mathrm{ESR}})\) , which is 45° at \(f_{\mathrm{ESR}}\) and almost nothing a decade below. If the zero is near the crossover \(f_c\) , it supplies for free part of the phase boost the compensator would have to give. That was the case in older bucks with electrolytic capacitors, whose ESR is tens of milliohms: with them, a type II compensator was enough. With ceramic capacitors, the ESR drops to a few milliohms, and the zero moves up to hundreds of kHz, above \(f_s/2\) . There it does not help: the digital loop does not even see frequencies above \(f_s/2\) (see Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH) ), and the compensator must give all the phase boost, with two zeros, like the The 2p2z compensator . Do not count on the ESR An electrolytic's ESR varies with temperature (it may double in the cold) and grows with aging. A design that relies on the ESR zero for its phase margin may lose it in winter or after a few years. And putting a ceramic in parallel, to lower the ripple, moves the zero and changes the whole plant. ESR on purpose A resistor is sometimes added in series with the capacitor just to create the zero. It works, but the cost shows in the output ripple and in the load-step response, which gains an instantaneous jump of \(\Delta I\cdot R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\) . In the converters In the lab's buck, C = 47 µF with an ESR of 5 mΩ: \[f_{\mathrm{ESR}} = \frac{1}{2\pi\cdot 5\,\text{m}\Omega\cdot 47\,\text{µF}} = 677\ \text{kHz}\] That is 3.4 times the 200 kHz switching frequency. At 8 kHz, the 2p2z's crossover, the zero gives 0.7° of phase; even at \(f_s/2\) = 100 kHz it gives only 8.4°. For the loop, the capacitor is ideal, and the compensator does all the work. summary: Two legs and one inductor that step the voltage down or up; the buck, boost and buck-boost modes, the plant that changes with the input and the mode the lab uses.
text: An 8 to 16 V battery feeding a 12 V bus must step the voltage down and up. The four-switch buck-boost does both with a single inductor, without inverting the output: a buck leg at the input (Q1 on top, Q2 below, node A) and a boost leg at the output (Q3 on top, Q4 below, node B), with the inductor between the two nodes. Three modes Buck. Q3 stays on and Q4 off; only the input leg switches. It is a buck: \(V = D\,V_{in}\) , the inductor current is the load's, and the plant has no right-half-plane zero. Boost. Q1 stays on and Q2 off; only the output leg switches. It is a boost: \(V = V_{in}/(1 - D)\) , with the right-half-plane zero . Buck-boost. Both legs switch together: G1 turns on Q1 and Q4, and the inductor receives the input; G2 turns on Q2 and Q3, and the inductor discharges into the output. From the volt-second balance, \(D\,V_{in} = D'\,V\) , that is, \(V/V_{in} = D/D'\) . The first two modes have lower losses, but the firmware must decide which mode it is in and switch modes when \(V_{in}\) crosses \(V\) , where each one's duty reaches its limit. The third covers the whole range with a single duty, without transitions. The price is that all four switches commutate every period and the inductor carries the input and output currents added together, \(I = I_o/D'\) . The lab's mode The lab's converter always runs in buck-boost mode: G1 drives Q1 and Q4, G2 drives Q2 and Q3. The firmware is the same as the buck's and the boost's, with one duty and one voltage loop. The small-signal model and every number on this site are for that mode. The plant in buck-boost mode With G1, the inductor sees \(+v_{in}\) ; with G2, \(-v\) . The averaged cell becomes \(L\,di_L/dt = d\,v_{in} - d'\,v - R_l\,i_L\) , and the capacitor receives \(d'\,i_L\) , as in the boost. Linearizing with \(\hat v_{in} = 0\) , \(\hat d\) switches the voltage \(V_{in} + V\) across the inductor, instead of the boost's \(V\) : \[G_{vd}(s) = Z_o(s)\,\frac{D'(V_{in} + V) - I\,(sL + R_l)}{sL + R_l + D'^2 Z_o(s)}, \qquad Z_o(s) = R \parallel \left(R_{ESR} + \frac{1}{sC}\right)\tag{1}\] ≡ Here \(R_l\) adds the inductor and the two switches always in series with it. title: Sizing L and C
summary: How to choose the buck's inductor and capacitor from the ripple specifications, the capacitor's RMS current and the load step.
text: This procedure uses the equations of Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM backwards: it starts from the specifications and arrives at L and C. At the end, we check the lab's buck. 1. Choose the current ripple and compute L Define the relative ripple \(r = \Delta i_L / I_{o,\max}\) . Values from 20 % to 40 % are the usual starting point: less calls for a large, slow inductor; more raises the peak, the core losses and the capacitor's RMS current. From the ripple equation , \[L = \frac{V_o\,(1 - D)}{r\,I_{o,\max}\,f_s}\] Use the highest input voltage: \(1 - D\) grows with \(V_{in}\) , and so does the ripple. Saturation Check the peak \(I_{o,\max} + \Delta i_L/2\) against the inductor's saturation current, not only against its rated current. The inductance of many powdered-iron inductors drops 20 % to 30 % with current, and the ripple rises in the same proportion. 2. Compute C and the maximum ESR from the voltage ripple With the specified output ripple \(\Delta v_o\) , split the budget between the two parts: \[C \ge \frac{\Delta i_L}{8\,f_s\,\Delta v_o}, \qquad R_{\mathrm{ESR}} \le \frac{\Delta v_o}{\Delta i_L}\] With ceramic capacitors, the ESR is a few milliohms and the capacitive part dominates. With electrolytics, the ESR usually dominates, and the capacitance ends up well above the minimum. Remember that the parts are out of phase: requiring each one below \(\Delta v_o\) already leaves some margin. Ceramic capacitance under bias An X5R or X7R ceramic loses a good part of its capacitance with the applied DC voltage. Use the manufacturer's curve at the output voltage, not the rated value. 3. Check the capacitor's RMS current The buck's output capacitor carries the triangular part of \(i_L\) : \[I_{C,\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{\Delta i_L}{\sqrt{12}}\tag{1}\] ≡ Compare it with the capacitor's rated RMS current (or that of the bank), at the working temperature. 4. Check the load step and the resonance Ripple rarely sets C. In a load step \(\Delta I\) , the capacitor supplies the difference until the loop reacts, and the loop reacts in about \(1/(2\pi f_c)\) . A first-order estimate of the dip is \[\Delta V \approx \frac{\Delta I}{2\pi\,f_c\,C}\] where \(f_c\) is the crossover frequency of the loop gain . Finally, compute the resonance \(f_0 = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})\) of the plant : it must lie well below \(f_s/2\) and preferably below \(f_c\) , because the compensator will have to cancel its pole pair. 5. title: The right-half-plane zero
summary: In the boost and the buck-boost, raising the duty first pulls the output down; this right-half-plane zero, at R·D'²/L, limits the crossover frequency.
text: In the buck, raising the duty raises the voltage applied to the LC filter, and the output rises. In the boost, the same action has two opposite effects. The main switch stays on longer, the inductor builds up more current, and the output will rise; but while the switch is on, the inductor is cut off from the output. At first, the inductor current is still the same, but it reaches the output during a smaller fraction of the period, \(D' - \hat d\) : the output receives \(I\hat d\) less and falls. Only later, when the inductor current grows, does it rise. A response that starts in the opposite direction to where it ends is the signature of a right-half-plane zero . The boost's plant From the averaged model in continuous conduction, with the losses \(R_l\) of the inductor and one switch, the capacitor with its ESR and the load \(R\) , the transfer function from the duty to the output is \[G_{vd}(s) = Z_o(s)\,\frac{D' V - I\,(sL + R_l)}{sL + R_l + D'^2 Z_o(s)}, \qquad Z_o(s) = R \parallel \left(R_{ESR} + \frac{1}{sC}\right)\tag{1}\] ≡ The numerator vanishes when \(D'V = I(sL + R_l)\) . With \(I = V/(RD')\) , the inductor current, the zero sits at \(s = +\omega_{\mathrm{RHP}}\) : \[\omega_{\mathrm{RHP}} = \frac{R\,D'^2 - R_l}{L} \approx \frac{R\,D'^2}{L}\tag{2}\] ≡ Right-half-plane zero A zero at \(s = +\omega_z\) , with \(\omega_z > 0\) . Like an ordinary zero, it makes the magnitude rise by 20 dB per decade above \(\omega_z\) ; but, like a pole, it lags the phase by up to \(90^\circ\) . In a step, it makes the response start in the wrong direction. Why it limits the crossover An ordinary zero in the left half-plane helps the compensator: it gives gain and phase lead. The right-half-plane zero gives the gain and takes the phase, like a delay. The compensator cannot cancel it, because that would take a pole in the right half-plane, an unstable controller. What is left is to cross well below it: at \(f_c\) , it already takes \(\arctan(f_c/f_{\mathrm{RHP}})\) , and this lag adds to the firmware's ( Computation and PWM delay ). Rules of thumb say to cross between a third and a fifth of the zero in the worst case: at \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/3\) , it takes 18.4° of phase; at \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/5\) , 11.3°. Neither is a limit: what decides is the margin at the worst corner, adding up the zero, the delay and the lead the compensator still gives there ( Robust design across the operating range ). And the worst case is the maximum load with the minimum input: smaller \(R\) and \(D'\) , lower zero. summary: The boost's plant in CCM has a DC gain of about V/D', a pair of poles that comes down with D' and a right-half-plane zero; the ADC also sees an ESR term and the firmware's delay.
text: In the buck, the duty only multiplies the input, and the plant is \(V_{in}\) times the LC filter ( The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\) ). In the boost, the averaged cell multiplies the state variables: the switch node is \(d'\,v\) and the current delivered to the output is \(d'\,i_L\) , with \(d' = 1 - d\) ( The averaged switch model ). The plant inherits three differences from this: the gain depends on \(D'\) , so does the resonance, and a right-half-plane zero appears. From the averaged model to the plant With \(R_l\) the inductor's resistance plus one switch's, the averaged equations of the inductor and the capacitor, perturbed and linearized with \(\hat v_{in} = 0\) , become \[(sL + R_l)\,\hat i_L = V\hat d - D'\hat v, \qquad \hat v = Z_o\,(D'\,\hat i_L - I\,\hat d)\] with \(Z_o = R \parallel (R_{ESR} + 1/sC)\) and \(I\) the average inductor current. The first term of each equation comes from \(d\) multiplying \(v\) and \(i_L\) : these are the \(V\hat d\) and \(I\hat d\) terms the buck does not have. Eliminating \(\hat i_L\) : \[G_{vd}(s) = Z_o(s)\,\frac{D' V - I\,(sL + R_l)}{sL + R_l + D'^2 Z_o(s)}, \qquad Z_o(s) = R \parallel \left(R_{ESR} + \frac{1}{sC}\right)\tag{1}\] ≡ DC gain, resonance and Q At \(s = 0\) , \(Z_o = R\) and, without losses, \(G_{vd}(0) = V/D'\) . At 48 V with \(D' \approx 0.25\) , that gives about 190 V per unit of duty: eight times the gain of the lab's buck. The denominator is the LC filter with the inductor seen through \(D'^2\) , as an inductance \(L/D'^2\) . The pair of poles lies at \[\omega_0 \approx \frac{D'}{\sqrt{LC}}, \qquad Q \approx \frac{\omega_0}{1/(RC) + R_l/L},\] and comes down when the input falls and \(D'\) shrinks. The damping comes from the load, \(1/(RC)\) , and from the losses, \(R_l/L\) . Effective inductance In the boost's averaged model, the inductor \(L\) seen from the output is \(L/D'^2\) . With \(D' = 0.25\) , the lab's 33 µH behave as 530 µH in the output filter: the resonance is four times lower than \(1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})\) . title: The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\)
summary: The buck's plant in CCM, from duty ratio to output voltage, is a second-order system with the LC resonance, a load-dependent Q and the ESR zero.
text: The linearized averaged model replaced the switch pair by a source \(\hat v_{sw} = V_{in}\,\hat d\) that drives the output filter. The plant is therefore \(V_{in}\) times that filter's transfer function. From the circuit to the transfer function The inductor and the series resistance form \(Z_L = sL + R_s\) , with \(R_s = R_L + R_{on}\) . The capacitor with its ESR, in parallel with the load, forms \(Z_o = (R_{\mathrm{ESR}} + 1/sC)\parallel R\) . The plant is a voltage divider: \[G_{vd}(s) = V_{in}\,\frac{Z_o}{Z_L + Z_o} = V_{in}\,\frac{R\,(1 + s R_{\mathrm{ESR}} C)}{\alpha_2 s^2 + \alpha_1 s + \alpha_0}\] with \[\alpha_2 = LC\,(R + R_{\mathrm{ESR}}), \qquad \alpha_0 = R + R_s\] \[\alpha_1 = L + C\left[R R_{\mathrm{ESR}} + R_s(R + R_{\mathrm{ESR}})\right]\] Arranged in the canonical second-order form: \[G_{vd}(s) = \frac{\hat v_o(s)}{\hat d(s)} = V_{in}\,\frac{R}{R + R_s}\;\frac{1 + s/\omega_{\mathrm{ESR}}}{1 + \dfrac{s}{Q\,\omega_0} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_0^2}}\tag{1}\] ≡ It has three ingredients: the DC gain \(V_{in}R/(R + R_s) \approx V_{in}\) , the LC's complex pole pair and the ESR zero. The resonance and the Q The pole pair sits at the filter's resonance, with a quality factor set by the damping: \[f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}, \qquad Q \approx \frac{1}{\dfrac{Z_0}{R} + \dfrac{R_s + R_{\mathrm{ESR}}}{Z_0}}, \qquad Z_0 = \sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}\tag{2}\] ≡ Quality factor \(Q\) measures how lightly damped the pole pair is. On the Bode plot, the magnitude rises about \(20\log_{10} Q\) dB above the DC gain at \(f_0\) , and the phase drops 180° over a band about \(f_0/Q\) wide. In time, the response rings at \(f_0\) and decays with a time constant \(2Q/\omega_0\) . Two sources of damping add like conductances: the load in parallel with the capacitor, with \(Q_R = R/Z_0\) , and the series resistances, with \(Q_s = Z_0/(R_s + R_{\mathrm{ESR}})\) . Hence the dependence on the load: heavy load (small R) damps more, and \(Q\) falls; light load (large R) damps less, and \(Q\) rises up to the limit \(Z_0/(R_s + R_{\mathrm{ESR}})\) , set by the losses alone; the DC gain and \(f_0\) barely change with the load. Above \(f_0\) , the magnitude falls 40 dB per decade and the phase stays near −180°. This is the phase the compensator must lift, with zeros near the resonance, for there to be phase margin at crossover (see Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins and The 2p2z compensator ). loading the figure… The buck's plant: resonant peak near 5 kHz and a 40 dB per decade roll-off; the phase includes the digital loop's (1+D)Tₛ delay. The peak depends on the load Design the compensator at the lightest load the converter will see. That is where the resonant peak is highest, and where the loop gain may cross 0 dB again with little phase. summary: The buck's complete interrupt: read the ADC, compute the error, run the 2p2z difference equation, saturate and write the CCR, in float and in fixed point, with the cycle budget and how to measure it.
text: This note puts together everything the trail has built. The 2p2z compensator becomes the difference equation below, the saturation of Anti-windup and duty saturation sits at the output, and the arithmetic is that of Q15 fixed point : \[u[k] = -a_1\,u[k-1] - a_2\,u[k-2] + b_0\,e[k] + b_1\,e[k-1] + b_2\,e[k-2]\tag{1}\] ≡ The sequence in each period The timer reaches the end of the period and generates the update event. That event triggers the ADC. The ADC finishes the conversion and calls the interrupt. The interrupt computes the error and the new duty, and saturates it. It writes the CCR. With preload on, the new value only takes effect in the next period. Step 4 is what scenario.cpp imitates with s->duty = s->pending : the duty computed from period \(k\) 's sample governs period \(k+1\) . With trailing-edge PWM, the edge that matters comes \(D\,T_s\) into that period, and the total delay is \((1 + D)\,T_s\) , the subject of Computation and PWM delay . Float variant (Cortex-M4F, M33) This is scenario.cpp 's logic, with the error in volts and the coefficients of the buck's default design. title: The 2p2z compensator
summary: The two-pole, two-zero compensator, a digital relative of the type III, designed by its poles and zeros, and its relation with the PID; with the buck's default design.
text: The buck's plant, above the LC resonance, has a phase near \(-180^\circ\) ( The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\) ), and the digital delay takes even more ( Computation and PWM delay ). An integrator alone would add \(-90^\circ\) , and the loop would have no margin. The compensator needs an integrator, to drive the steady-state error to zero, and two zeros, to give phase back at the crossover. That is the 2p2z : two poles, two zeros. \[C(z) = K\,\frac{(1 - z_1 z^{-1})(1 - z_2 z^{-1})}{(1 - z^{-1})(1 - p\,z^{-1})}, \qquad z_i = e^{-\omega_{zi} T_s}, \quad p = e^{-\omega_p T_s}\tag{1}\] ≡ The two poles are the integrator, at \(z = 1\) , and a real high-frequency pole \(p\) . It is the digital version of the analog type III compensator, which has two high-frequency poles instead of one. Design by poles and zeros Each root has a job, and the design is done on the Bode plot of the loop gain : Integrator ( \(z = 1\) ): infinite gain at DC, zero steady-state error at the sample. Two zeros near or below the LC resonance: each gives back up to \(+90^\circ\) . Below the resonance, they already give almost all their lead when the plant's phase plunges. Lower zeros give more phase at \(f_c\) , but they lower the gain between the integrator and the resonance, and the loop becomes slow to correct errors in that band. High-frequency pole : limits the gain above the crossover, where there is only ripple and quantization noise ( ADC quantization ). When the ESR zero falls inside the band, the pole is placed on it to cancel it ( The ESR zero ). Gain \(K\) : chosen last, so that \(|T_L| = 1\) at \(f_c\) . The zeros and the pole go to \(z\) by matching ( The bilinear (Tustin) transform and prewarping ): \(z_i = e^{-\omega_{zi}T_s}\) and \(p = e^{-\omega_p T_s}\) . Expanding the numerator and the denominator, \[C(z) = \frac{b_0 + b_1 z^{-1} + b_2 z^{-2}}{1 + a_1 z^{-1} + a_2 z^{-2}},\] the firmware receives \(b_0 = K\) , \(b_1 = -K(z_1+z_2)\) , \(b_2 = K z_1 z_2\) , \(a_1 = -(1+p)\) and \(a_2 = p\) , and runs the difference equation \[u[k] = -a_1\,u[k-1] - a_2\,u[k-2] + b_0\,e[k] + b_1\,e[k-1] + b_2\,e[k-2]\tag{2}\] ≡ This is the velocity form : the integrator lives in the two past \(u\) terms. Since the integrator at \(z = 1\) forces \(1 + a_1 + a_2 = 0\) , the equation can be rewritten as \(u[k] - u[k-1] = a_2\,(u[k-1] - u[k-2]) + b_0\,e[k] + b_1\,e[k-1] + b_2\,e[k-2]\) : the firmware computes the increment \(\Delta u\) and adds it to the previous duty. title: ADC quantization
summary: The ADC reads the output in steps of \(q = V_{FS}/(2^N - 1)\): the step, the quantization noise, the reference written as a code and the sampling instant decide what the loop can regulate.
text: The digital controller doesn't see the output voltage: it sees an integer. In Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH) , sampling made time discrete; here the A/D converter (ADC) makes the amplitude discrete, and everything the firmware knows about \(v_o\) goes through that rounding. The step (LSB) ADC step The step, or LSB (least significant bit), is the smallest change of the measured voltage that changes the code read. An \(N\) -bit ADC has \(2^N\) codes, from 0 to \(2^N - 1\) : code 0 reads 0 V, the largest reads full scale, and between them the measuring range is divided into \(2^N - 1\) steps. The ADC pin only accepts 0 to \(V_{\mathrm{ADC}}\) (3.3 V on an STM32). To measure a larger output, a resistive divider of ratio \(k_{\mathrm{div}}\) scales the voltage down, and the range referred to the output becomes \(V_{FS} = V_{\mathrm{ADC}}/k_{\mathrm{div}}\) : \[q = \frac{V_{FS}}{2^{N} - 1} = \frac{V_{\mathrm{ADC}}}{(2^{N} - 1)\,k_{\mathrm{div}}}\tag{1}\] ≡ In the buck, \(V_{FS}\) = 20 V and \(N\) = 12 bits. The divider has \(k_{\mathrm{div}} = 3.3/20 = 0.165\) , and \[q = \frac{20\ \text{V}}{4095} = 4.884\ \text{mV at the output} \qquad \left(\frac{3.3\ \text{V}}{4095} = 0.806\ \text{mV at the pin}\right).\] Code \(k\) reads \(k \cdot 20/4095\) V: the largest, 4095, reads exactly 20 V. That is the scale of the simulations' firmware ( scenario.cpp ), which rounds the sample to the nearest code. The range needs headroom above the nominal output, to see the overshoot and to protect against overvoltage, but every volt of headroom makes \(q\) coarser. Quantization noise When the voltage moves many steps between samples, the rounding error \(\varepsilon = v - q\cdot\text{code}\) spreads evenly between \(-q/2\) and \(q/2\) . The variance of that uniform distribution is \[\sigma_\varepsilon^2 = \frac{1}{q}\int_{-q/2}^{q/2} \varepsilon^2\, d\varepsilon = \frac{q^2}{12}, \qquad \sigma_\varepsilon = \frac{q}{\sqrt{12}} \approx 0.29\,q .\] In the buck, \(\sigma_\varepsilon = 4.884/\sqrt{12} = 1.41\) mV rms. This white-noise model holds during transients. In steady state it fails: the output barely changes, and the quantization error becomes a fixed error, or a repeating pattern. The same goes for a measurement: a signal that moves the sample by less than one code is lost in the rounding, which is why the sine that measures the loop gain grows with frequency ( Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty ). What the zero-error band means For the controller, every output within a band of width \(q\) around the reference's code gives the same error. Inside that band the integrator has nothing to correct. The regulation's resolution is, at best, \(\pm q/2 = \pm 2.44\) mV at 9 V, or 0.03 %. That is resolution, not accuracy. The divider's tolerance and the ADC's gain and offset errors are worth tens of steps (see exercise 1). title: Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost
summary: In the boost and the buck-boost, the sample taken just before G1 turns on sits above the output's average and reads an ESR term that changes the plant; with it, the effective delay that fits QSPICE is (1 + 0.6·D)·Tₛ.
text: The averaged model describes the output's average over a period. The ADC does not read the average: it reads the voltage at one instant, and what that instant sees depends on the waveform. In the buck, the sample at the start of the period falls near the ripple's valley, a few millivolts below the average ( Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH) ). In the boost and the buck-boost, the difference is larger and, besides, it changes with the duty and with the current: it becomes part of the plant. What the sample reads This site's firmware triggers the ADC at the start of each period, just before G1 turns on. In the boost, G1 is the main switch: until then, G2 was conducting, and the capacitor received the inductor current minus the load's. Two effects add up: The capacitor ripple. While G1 conducts, only the capacitor feeds the load, and the voltage falls by \(\Delta v_C = I_o D T_s/C\) ; while G2 conducts, it rises again. The sample catches the end of the rise, the peak: \(\Delta v_C/2\) above the average. The ESR drop. On average, the capacitor receives \(d'\,i_L - i_o = 0\) . At the sampling instant, it receives \(i_L - i_o\) : the whole inductor current, \(d\,i_L\) more than the average. The sample reads \(R_{ESR}\,d\,i_L\) more, minus the valley of the current ripple. The first effect is nearly constant and only shifts the regulated value: the loop regulates the sample, and the average sits below it. The second changes with \(d\) and with \(i_L\) , and its linearization enters the plant: \[\hat v_s = \hat v + R_{ESR}\left(D\,\hat i_L + I\,\hat d\right)\tag{1}\] ≡ Plant seen by the ADC The transfer function from the duty to the sample , not to the average output. It is the one that enters the loop gain. In this site's boost and buck-boost, it is \(G_{vd}\) plus the ESR term, times the firmware's delay. The \(R_{ESR}\,I\,\hat d\) term does not fall with frequency. title: Anti-windup and duty saturation
summary: When the duty hits its limit, the integrator must not keep accumulating error: the integrator clamp, the 2p2z velocity form, back-calculation, the reference slew and the derivative kick.
text: The duty has limits, and the linear 2p2z compensator doesn't know it. This note shows, step by step, how to keep an integrator from accumulating error while the output is saturated. 1. Saturate the duty Every controller ends with a clamp to \([d_{\min}, d_{\max}]\) . In the buck, \(d_{\min}\) = 0 and \(d_{\max}\) = 0.9. Besides the physical limit between 0 and 1, a maximum below 1 leaves time for the driver's bootstrap capacitor to recharge and an off interval to measure current. With \(d_{\max} = 0.9\) , the buck only delivers 15 V if the input is above about 17 V. 2. Understand windup While the output is saturated, the loop is open: raising the command changes nothing. The integrator keeps adding the error, and that excess must be discharged later, with an error of the opposite sign, that is, with overshoot. The PID of scenario.cpp and buck_pid.cpp uses the simplest solution, the integrator clamp : the state is limited to the same range as the duty. integ += KI * T * err; if (integ < DMIN) integ = DMIN; /* anti-windup by clamping */ if (integ > DMAX) integ = DMAX; d = KP * err + integ + deriv; if (d < DMIN) d = DMIN; if (d > DMAX) d = DMAX; The clamp prevents the worst, but the integrator can still sit at \(d_{\max}\) when the operating point needs much less, and the output overshoots the reference while it unwinds. The example at the end of section 3 measures that overshoot in the boost. 3. Or use the velocity form The 2p2z in C computes each duty from the two previous ones ( equation Difference equation of the 2p2z ) and stores the saturated ones. No state grows past the limits: the form is anti-windup by construction. It has one flaw, though. When a jump in the error saturates the duty, the next period's term \(b_1\,e[k-1]\) takes back the whole kick, which was never applied, and the duty plunges the other way. Measured in the boost: clamp versus velocity form QSPICE simulations of the boost, with the netlist and firmware of the scenarios. The same PID ( \(K_P\) = 0.0114, \(K_I\) = 18.2, \(K_D\) = 1.75 µs/V, \(T_F\) = 7.96 µs) runs with the integrator clamp and as a 2p2z in velocity form, with the same transfer function. Settling, here, means entering the ±2 % band around 48 V for good. Input dropout. At 6 V, not even \(d_{\max} = 0.85\) is enough: the output stalls at 36.6 V, and the integrator sits on the clamp at 0.85, while the operating point at 12 V needs 0.76. The input then returns to 12 V at 10 V/ms. PID with clamp: another 450 µs at the limit, 33.8 A in the inductor, a 56.0 V peak, and settling in 1.79 ms. That is windup. Velocity form: 240 µs at the limit, 21.5 A, a 50.4 V peak, and settling in 0.96 ms. Reference step from 40 to 48 V, without slew. The derivative kick takes the duty to 0.85. PID with clamp: four periods at 0.85, no overshoot, and settling in 1.0 ms. Velocity form: this is the flaw above. The duty drops to 0.09 and stays at zero for two periods, the inductor current goes to −34.7 A, and the output plunges to 7.7 V.

title: Computation and PWM delay
summary: From the ADC sample to the PWM edge it moves, \((1 + D)\,T_s\) go by in this firmware, and this delay costs \(360^\circ\, f\,(1 + D)\,T_s\) of phase at the crossover.
text: In an analog loop, a change at the output reaches the PWM comparator almost at once. In a digital one, the information travels a chain: the ADC converts, the interrupt computes, the PWM register is updated and, only then, an edge of the pulse moves. Each stage delays the response, and a pure delay \(t_d\) is \(e^{-s t_d}\) : it leaves the magnitude of the loop gain alone, but takes phase. The chain in this site's firmware Period \(k\) starts at \(t = kT_s\) : Sample and conversion. The timer triggers the ADC at \(kT_s\) ( Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH) ). The conversion takes from hundreds of nanoseconds to a few microseconds. Computation. The end-of-conversion interrupt runs the PID or the 2p2z and writes the new duty to the compare register (CCR). Update in the next period. With preload on, the new CCR only takes effect at the next update event, at \((k+1)T_s\) . This guarantees a whole pulse with the old value, even if the computation runs late, and costs one period. The modulated edge. In a trailing-edge (sawtooth) PWM, the switch turns on at the start of the period and off at \((k+1+D)T_s\) . Only that edge depends on \(d\) ; the duty perturbation enters the plant there, \(DT_s\) after the start. Adding up, the delay from the sample to the edge it moves is \[\varphi_d(f) = -360^\circ\, f\, t_d, \qquad t_d = (1 + D)\,T_s\tag{1}\] ≡ The \(DT_s\) term plays the role of the zero-order hold: instead of the ZOH's average half period, the modulator delays up to the edge that actually moves. The PWM modulator also has a gain: in a real timer, \(d = \mathrm{CCR}/\mathrm{ARR}\) , and an 850-step counter (170 MHz for 200 kHz) gives \(1/850\) per step. In this firmware the duty is computed per unit, the modulator's gain is 1 and \(G_{vd}\) already includes \(V_{in}\) . The resolution of those steps is the subject of DPWM resolution and limit cycles . For those coming from the reference course There, the digital loop's delay is "ZOH, \(-\omega T_s/2\) , plus \(z^{-1}\) when the update goes to the next cycle", and no "PWM delay" is added to the ZOH. The rule is the same as here, written another way: that ZOH is the modulator, the time from the instant the new duty takes effect to the edge it moves (or to the midpoint of the two edges, when both move). In that course's symmetric PWM, with the update at the triangle's peak or valley, that midpoint lies half a period after the update for any \(D\) , and the modulator is worth \(T_s/2\) . In this site's trailing-edge PWM, only the falling edge moves, \(DT_s\) after the start of the period. Hence \[(1+D)\,T_s = \underbrace{T_s}_{z^{-1}} + \underbrace{T_s/2}_{\text{ZOH}} + \underbrace{(D-\tfrac12)\,T_s}_{\text{edge position}}.\] With \(D = 0.5\) , both counts give \(1.5\,T_s\) . In the buck, with \(D = 0.375\) , "ZOH plus \(z^{-1}\) " counts \(1.5\,T_s\) instead of \(1.375\,T_s\) : \(1.8^\circ\) more phase at 8 kHz, and the 2p2z's margin comes out \(39.6^\circ\) instead of \(41.3^\circ\) . title: DPWM resolution and limit cycles
summary: The duty also moves in steps: when the step it causes at the output is larger than the ADC step, the loop has nowhere to settle and oscillates in a limit cycle.
text: In ADC quantization , the measurement of the output moved in steps. So does the actuator: the digital PWM (DPWM) only produces a finite number of duty values, and the two quantizers together can keep the loop from settling. The DPWM step A timer counts clock pulses from 0 to the end of the period, and the PWM output changes when the counter passes the compare value (the CCR register). The duty can only be \(\mathrm{CCR}/N_{\mathrm{PWM}}\) : \[N_{\mathrm{PWM}} = \frac{f_{\mathrm{clk}}}{f_s}, \qquad \Delta D = \frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{PWM}}}, \qquad n_{\mathrm{PWM}} = \log_2 N_{\mathrm{PWM}}\tag{1}\] ≡ On an STM32G4 with the timer at 170 MHz and \(f_s\) = 200 kHz, there are \(170/0.2 = 850\) counts per period: \(\Delta D = 1/850\) , or \(\log_2 850 = 9.7\) bits. In center-aligned mode (the counter goes up and down) 425 counts remain, 8.7 bits. The resolution gets worse with the switching frequency: doubling \(f_s\) costs one bit. High-resolution timers solve this. The STM32G4's HRTIM divides each 170 MHz cycle into 32 (184 ps steps), which is like counting at 5.44 GHz: 27,200 counts at 200 kHz, or 14.7 bits. Other manufacturers have similar peripherals. The step at the output In steady state, changing the duty by \(\Delta D\) moves the output by \(|G_{vd}(0)|\,\Delta D\) , with \(G_{vd}\) the plant of The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\) . In the buck, \(G_{vd}(0) \approx V_{in}\) : \[\Delta V_{\mathrm{DPWM}} = \frac{24\ \text{V}}{850} = 28.2\ \text{mV} \qquad \text{against} \qquad q = 4.884\ \text{mV}.\] One step of the ordinary timer moves the output almost six ADC steps. No CCR value puts the output inside the ADC's zero-error band, which is only 4.884 mV wide. loading the figure… The buck's two quantizers: a 12-bit ADC and a 10-bit DPWM (1024 counts, 23.4 mV per step at the output). Change the resolutions and see when a DPWM level appears inside the zero-error band. Limit cycle Limit cycle A sustained periodic oscillation of a nonlinear system, with no external excitation. In a quantized loop, the output alternates between DPWM levels because none of them cancels the error read. The mechanism is simple. The integrator accumulates the error and raises the duty one step; the output rises 28 mV and jumps over the band; the error changes sign, the integrator goes down, and the story repeats. The linear analysis of Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins doesn't predict it: the loop can have good margins and still oscillate, with an amplitude of the order of the DPWM step. Peterchev and Sanders (2003) gave three conditions for removing steady-state limit cycles: a DPWM finer than the ADC , so that a DPWM level exists inside the zero-error band. They suggest one extra bit, which gives two DPWM levels per ADC level; an integrator in the controller, with limited gain . title: Q15 fixed point
summary: Without an FPU, coefficients and signals become scaled integers: Qm.n formats, Q15 multiplication with rounding and saturation, and the scaling of the buck's 2p2z coefficients.
text: The 2p2z compensator has coefficients such as 0.23114 and −0.43413. With a floating-point unit, they go into the code as they are. Without one, each number becomes an integer with an implicit scale. Float or fixed point? With an FPU (Cortex-M4F, M7, M33 with FPU, such as the STM32G4, F4 and H7): use float . The single-precision FPU multiplies and adds in one to three cycles (typical datasheet figures, not measured here), and the 24-bit mantissa is more than enough for this loop. Without an FPU (Cortex-M0 and M0+, such as the STM32G0 and C0): every float operation becomes a library call of, typically, tens of cycles. With a 5 µs period and a 64 MHz core, there are only 320 cycles per period. Here fixed point is used. Hidden double precision On a single-precision FPU, 0.5 is a double , and x * 0.5 is computed in software. Write 0.5f , and compile with -Wdouble-promotion so the compiler points out the cases. The Qm.n format Qm.n format A signed integer \(X\) represents \(x = X/2^n\) : \(n\) fraction bits and \(m\) integer bits besides the sign, \(1 + m + n\) bits in all. Q15 (or Q0.15) is the int16_t read as a fraction, from −1 to \(1 - 2^{-15}\) , in steps of \(3.05\times10^{-5}\) . \[x = \frac{X}{2^{n}}, \quad X \in \left[-2^{m+n},\; 2^{m+n}-1\right], \qquad Z = \left\lfloor \frac{X\,Y + 2^{n-1}}{2^{n}} \right\rfloor\tag{1}\] ≡ Q2.13 covers −4 to 4 in steps of \(1.22\times10^{-4}\) : it trades resolution for headroom. The product of two Q15 numbers has 30 fraction bits and fits in 32 bits. To return to Q15, add half a step ( \(2^{14}\) ) and shift by 15 bits: #include <stdint.h> static inline int16_t sat16(int32_t x) /* saturate instead of wrapping */ { return x > INT16_MAX ? INT16_MAX : x < INT16_MIN ? INT16_MIN : (int16_t)x; } static inline int16_t q15_mul(int16_t a, int16_t b) { int32_t p = (int32_t)a * b; /* Q30: the cast comes before the multiplication */ p += 1 << 14; /* round instead of truncating */ return sat16(p >> 15); /* -1 * -1 = +1 doesn't fit in Q15: saturate */ } Three pitfalls Overflow: without saturation, \(0.9 + 0.2\) in Q15 becomes \(-0.9\) . A duty that jumps from 0.9 to −0.9 is the worst possible error. On the Cortex-M3 and M4, CMSIS offers __SSAT(x, 16) , which saturates in one instruction. Truncation: p >> 15 without the half step always rounds down, a bias that the integrator accumulates. Shifting negatives: in C99, >> of a negative number is implementation-defined. In GCC for ARM it is arithmetic; check your compiler. To add several products, use a 64-bit accumulator. Each Q15 × Q15 product already takes 31 bits, and two of them added can overflow 32 bits. On the Cortex-M4, the SMLAL instruction multiplies and accumulates in 64 bits in one cycle, according to the core's manual. The M0 has no such instruction, and the compiler emulates the operation with several. title: Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty
summary: A sine added to the duty in the firmware gives the loop gain as \(-C/U\); the amplitude has to grow with frequency so the ADC sample moves several codes, and a second measurement at half the amplitude shows whether the point is linear.
text: The site's models were checked against the switched circuit in QSPICE, with the scenarios' firmware. This note shows how: where the sine goes in, how the loop gain comes out, and the two precautions that separate a reliable measurement from one that only measures the ADC's rounding. The injection Inside the interrupt, the firmware adds a small sine \(x\) to the duty \(c\) the controller computed, and the PWM uses \(u = c + x\) . The sine goes around the loop: it moves the output, the ADC sample, the error and, one period later, \(c\) itself. With \(T_L = G_c\,G_{vd}\,H\) and the error defined as reference minus sample, the part of \(c\) at the sine's frequency is \(\hat c = -T_L\,\hat u\) , and \[T_L = -\frac{C}{U},\] with \(C\) and \(U\) the Fourier components of \(c\) and \(u\) at the injected frequency. Since both signals are read at the same point in the firmware, the computation and PWM delays enter the measurement with no extra care. The same computation with the sample \(V\) in place of \(C\) gives the plant as the ADC sees it, \(V/U\) , without the compensator. In the lab, tools/qspice_loop_check.py records \(c\) , \(u\) and the sample every period, waits 30 ms for the LC resonance, which rings for tens of milliseconds in open loop, and computes \(C\) and \(U\) over 40 whole cycles of the sine, with a Hann window against the leakage of that ringing. On a board, the procedure is the same: the firmware injects and records \(c\) and \(u\) , and the computation is done offline. The amplitude grows with frequency The sine has to be small so as not to leave the linear regime, but the ADC sample only moves in steps of \(q = V_{FS}/(2^N - 1)\) ( ADC quantization ). Above the resonance, the plant falls, and a fixed amplitude that is enough at low frequency ends up moving the sample by less than one code: what gets measured then is the rounding, not the plant. The way out is to choose, at each frequency, the amplitude that, according to the model, moves the sample by about 10 codes: \[a(f) = \min\!\left(0.06,\ \max\!\left(0.004,\ \frac{10\,q}{|P(f)|}\right)\right),\] with \(P\) the plant from the duty to the sample, in volts per unit of duty. The floor, 0.004, keeps the sine small near the resonance, where a large one would reverse the inductor current at light load; the ceiling is 0.06, or less when the applied duty, which swings by \(a/|1+T_L|\) , would come close to its limits: it may use at most 80 % of its distance to \(D_{min}\) or \(D_{max}\) . In the boost at 10 V input, from 5.5 to 7 kHz, 0.06 would take the duty to 0.87, above the 0.85 limit. The linearity check In a linear system, the gain does not depend on the amplitude. So each frequency is measured again with half the sine: if \(T_L\) changes by more than 0.5 dB or 3°, the point is not linear and must not be used to check the model. title: Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
summary: The loop gain \(T_L = G_c\,G_{vd}\,H\), the crossover frequency and the phase and gain margins, and what they predict about overshoot and ringing.
text: A voltage loop reads the output, compares it with the reference and corrects the duty. If we open the loop at any point and follow a signal once around it, it goes through three blocks in series: the controller \(G_c\) , the plant \(G_{vd}\) from the small-signal note and the sensor \(H\) . Their product is the loop gain : \[G_{vd}(s) = \frac{\hat v_o(s)}{\hat d(s)} = V_{in}\,\frac{R}{R + R_s}\;\frac{1 + s/\omega_{\mathrm{ESR}}}{1 + \dfrac{s}{Q\,\omega_0} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_0^2}}\tag{1}\] ≡ \[T_L(s) = G_c(s)\,G_{vd}(s)\,H\tag{2}\] ≡ Loop gain \(T_L(s)\) is the gain of a signal that goes once around the loop. With the loop closed, the output follows the reference by \(T_L/(1+T_L)\) , and a disturbance at the output is divided by \(1 + T_L\) . Where \(|T_L| \gg 1\) , the output follows the reference; where \(|T_L| \ll 1\) , the loop does nothing. Stability is analyzed on \(T_L\) , not on the closed loop. Crossover and margins Crossover frequency \(f_c\) : where \(|T_L| = 1\) (0 dB). In order of magnitude, it is the closed loop's bandwidth; the higher it is, the faster the loop corrects. Phase margin (PM): \(180^\circ + \angle T_L(j2\pi f_c)\) . It is how much extra phase lag the loop still tolerates at \(f_c\) before it oscillates. Gain margin (GM): \(-|T_L|_{\mathrm{dB}}\) at the frequency where the phase crosses \(-180^\circ\) . It is how much the gain can still rise. Both measure the distance from \(T_L\) to the point \(-1\) , where \(1 + T_L = 0\) and the loop oscillates by itself. At the crossover, \(|1 + T_L| = 2\sin(\mathrm{PM}/2)\) , so the closed loop peaks near \(f_c\) at about \[\left|\frac{T_L}{1+T_L}\right|_{f_c} = \frac{1}{2\sin(\mathrm{PM}/2)}.\] That is what the margin predicts in the time domain: with a PM of 60° there is no peak, the overshoot is small and the ringing dies out in a few cycles of \(f_c\) . With 30°, the peak is already close to 6 dB, and every step rings at a frequency near \(f_c\) . A rough rule for the damping of the pole pair near the crossover is \(\zeta \approx \mathrm{PM}/100\) ( From margin to damping: the ζ ≈ PM/100 rule and where it fails ); with the 2p2z, it misses by up to 10 % in the boost, up to 23 % in the buck-boost and 31 % in the buck. In all three converters, this pair rules the load step, but it is not dominant: the closed loop also has a slow real pole, near 470 Hz in the buck, 200 Hz in the boost and 330 Hz in the buck-boost, which makes the tail and sets the settling time when the reference changes. loading the figure… Loop gain of the buck with the default 2p2z: crossover, phase margin and gain margin Why \(f_c\) cannot rise at will Three things limit the crossover of a converter controlled by a microcontroller: Sampling. summary: How a digital PWM takes the new duty from the CCR's preload to the edge it moves, and the delay that follows, \(t_d = t_c + t_m\): "half-period ZOH plus \(z^{-1}\)" and "\((1 + D)\,T_s\)" are the same model for different PWMs; adding the two counts the modulator twice.
text: In a digital PWM, the firmware does not move the edge: it writes the new duty to the CCR's preload (the shadow register), and a timer update event copies that value to the active register, the one the carrier is compared with. In a trailing-edge PWM, with a sawtooth carrier, the update is the counter reset. In a symmetric PWM, with a triangle carrier, it is the peak, the valley or both. Only then does the edge move, and the loop's delay is the time from the sample to that edge. The figure shows both cases, period by period. loading the figure… Timing diagram of the trailing-edge PWM (top) and the symmetric one (bottom): carrier and CCR, gate, ADC sample, interrupt, write to the CCR and update event; with the step, the edges that sample k moves and the delays t_c, t_m and t_d, in Tₛ The reference course counts this delay as "ZOH, \(-\omega T_s/2\) , plus \(z^{-1}\) when the update goes to the next cycle", without adding a "PWM delay" to the ZOH. This site counts \((1 + D)\,T_s\) ( Computation and PWM delay ). Both counts are right, each for its own PWM; the error is to mix them. One delay, two parts In a digital PWM with one update per period, the delay from the sample to the plant is \[t_d = t_c + t_m,\] where \(t_c\) runs from the sample to the instant the new duty takes effect (the update event), and \(t_m\) from that instant to the edge it moves (or to the midpoint of the two edges, when both move). In small signals, the edge shifted by \(\hat d\,T_s\) adds to the switched voltage a pulse of height \(V_{in}\) and width \(\hat d\,T_s\) ; to first order, an impulse at the edge's instant. So the modulator acts as a pure delay \(t_m\) , with exact phase in the baseband term. What is left are folded terms, negligible in the buck up to about \(f_s/10\) . In an analog PWM, the edge responds to the instantaneous value of the modulating signal, and this \(t_m\) does not exist: the modulator has only its gain \(1/V_M\) . Trailing edge, update in the next period This is this site's firmware: sample at \(kT_s\) , CCR preload, switch turning on at the start of the period. Then \(t_c = T_s\) , and only the falling edge moves, \(DT_s\) after the start: \(t_m = DT_s\) . Splitting off the half period, \[(1+D)\,T_s = \underbrace{T_s}_{z^{-1}} + \underbrace{T_s/2}_{\text{ZOH}} + \underbrace{(D-\tfrac12)\,T_s}_{\text{edge position}}.\] The "ZOH" is already inside the \(DT_s\) term. With \(D = 0.5\) , both counts give \(1.5\,T_s\) ; with \(D < 0.5\) , "ZOH plus \(z^{-1}\) " counts too much delay and stays on the safe side; with \(D > 0.5\) , it counts too little and is optimistic. With a leading edge, \(t_m = (1-D)\,T_s\) , and the error's sign flips.
